meta.competitionFrequencyPerWeek: 1–2 meets per week at peak season; single-race duration 10–50 s
meta.notes: Sprinting (100–400 m) is the most power-demanding track discipline. 100 m is near-pure neuromuscular speed; 400 m adds a decisive lactate-tolerance component. The gym is CRITICAL: maximal strength and explosive power directly drive horizontal force application, acceleration mechanics, and top-end velocity. The hamstring is the signature injury — protective gym programming (Nordic curls, RDL, hip hinge) is non-negotiable. Olympic lifts, depth jumps, bounds, and sled work all have direct transfer. Non-propulsive mass must be minimised — lean, explosive, event-specific.

maxStrength.why: High maximal force output underpins horizontal force application at ground contact; stronger athletes produce greater peak forces in shorter contact times.

relativeStrength.why: Strength per kilogram directly scales acceleration — carrying non-propulsive mass without proportional force output limits sprint velocity.

explosivePower.why: The defining physical quality of sprinting — rate of force development and peak power at ground contact determine both acceleration and top speed. The gym must prioritise this above all.

reactiveStrength.why: Maximal-velocity sprinting involves contact times of ~80–100 ms — the stretch-shortening cycle and leg stiffness are decisive at top speed; reactive strength index is a strong performance correlate.
reactiveStrength.source: Markovic 2007 (plyometric-training meta-analysis); Seitz 2014 (lower-body strength → sprint transfer)

sprintSpeed.why: Sprint speed IS the performance outcome — improving maximal velocity is the primary goal of the entire training system.

acceleration.why: 0–30 m acceleration phase is decisive in all sprint events; force orientation (horizontal force production) during this phase largely determines race outcome.

deceleration.why: Velocity maintenance in the late 100–400 m requires resisting deceleration; some strength in this quality, but not a primary driver.
deceleration.source: sprint-fatigue and velocity-maintenance literature; expert consensus

changeOfDirection.why: Minimal — sprinters run straight lines (lane running); COD is irrelevant to performance and a low training priority.

aerobicEndurance.why: Low direct competition relevance (events last 10–50 s). A minimal aerobic base supports general training capacity, recovery, and 400 m lactic buffering but is not a performance limiter.

anaerobicEndurance.why: Glycolytic capacity is decisive in the 200–400 m — lactate production and buffering determine the ability to sustain speed in the later stages of the race.

repeatSprintAbility.why: Heats + semis + finals scheduling requires some capacity to repeat maximal efforts across a meet; lower priority than peak power/speed.

mobility.why: Hip extension, hip flexor flexibility, and ankle dorsiflexion range directly affect stride length, ground-contact mechanics, and injury risk (especially hamstring).
mobility.source: sprint-biomechanics literature; Askling hamstring prevention work

stability.why: Pelvis-lumbar stability and single-leg stability at ground contact underpin efficient force transfer and reduce injury risk during high-speed running.
stability.source: sprint-mechanics and core-stability literature; expert consensus

rotationalPower.why: Arm drive and trunk counter-rotation contribute to sprint mechanics; a secondary quality — trained via core anti-rotation and medicine-ball work.

gripStrength.why: Minimal relevance — block start requires grip but is not a limiter; no implement.

neckStrength.why: Very low — no collision; head position matters for mechanics but neck strength is not a sprint limiter.

balance.why: Single-leg stance phases and block start require balance; contributes modestly to mechanics and prehab work.

coordination.why: Sprint-specific coordination — arm drive, leg cycle mechanics, block start posture, and A-skip/B-skip drills — is highly trained and strongly predictive of performance.

durability.why: Sprint training loads are high-intensity but low-volume; acute injury (hamstring strain) dominates over cumulative overuse. Some durability in connective tissue is needed but is secondary to peak power development.

energySystems.workToRestRatio: 1:20–40 for maximal speed work; 1:6–10 for speed-endurance; race is a single maximal effort
energySystems.matchDemands: Highly event-dependent: 100 m ≈ ATP-PC dominant (≥50% phosphocreatine resynthesis contributes, maximal power throughout); 200 m ≈ glycolytic/ATP-PC mixed; 400 m ≈ predominantly glycolytic (lactate production peak) with meaningful aerobic contribution (~20–30%) in final stages. Values above are a 200–400 m weighted midpoint. ATP-PC is the primary fuel for the first 5–7 s; glycolysis dominates from ~7 s onward.
energySystems.heartRateProfile: Near-maximal HR achieved by race end; brief duration means cardiovascular output lags muscular demand in the 100 m — the race is over before aerobic machinery reaches full contribution.
energySystems.fatigueProfile: Velocity decrement late in the 200–400 m reflects lactate accumulation and phosphocreatine depletion; at 100 m, fatigue is largely neuromuscular/CNS. The body does not 'fail' aerobically — it fails glycolytically or via peak power output decline.
energySystems.source: Gastin 2001 energy-system contribution during maximal exercise
energySystems.notes: Because the spectrum is event-dependent, the engine should read the event archetype (positions) rather than a single split.

movementProfile.jointLoading: Extreme posterior-chain loading at heel-strike to toe-off — hamstring and gluteal force requirements during late swing and early stance are enormous at maximal velocity. Achilles/calf loaded at push-off. Hip flexors loaded during swing recovery. Knee under extension/flexion force at contact.
movementProfile.groundContacts: 100–250 contacts per race; maximal force per contact at top speed. Training involves thousands of high-force contacts per week.
movementProfile.landingDemands: High-velocity, stiff-knee plyometric landings in training (depth jumps, bounds); tight ground-contact times essential for maximal-velocity mechanics.
movementProfile.jumping: Block start is explosive; plyometric training (depth jumps, bounds, pogos) is integral to sprint development.
movementProfile.rotating: Arm counter-rotation and trunk anti-rotation; minimal overt rotation.
movementProfile.repeatedImpacts: High-force, high-velocity ground impacts in every track session. Hamstring under extreme eccentric load in late swing phase — the primary injury mechanism.
movementProfile.asymmetricLoading: Block start has a push-off lead/trail leg asymmetry; stride asymmetry common; monitor bilateral strength and contact-time balance.
dominantMuscleGroups: hamstrings (biceps femoris — the dominant injury target)
commonDeficiencies: hamstring eccentric strength relative to quadriceps
weak glute medius / hip abductor stability
insufficient relative strength (force production per kg)

common.name: Hamstring strain (biceps femoris — acute)
common.incidence: highest in sprinting — THE signature sprint injury; 26–29% of all track injuries in some registries
common.severity: moderate-high (grade I–III; grade II/III = weeks to months out)
common.mechanism: High-speed eccentric loading of the biceps femoris long head during late swing phase when the muscle is simultaneously lengthening under neural demand; also occurs at block start (proximal hamstring). Inadequate eccentric strength a primary modifiable risk factor.
highRiskTissues: biceps femoris long head (proximal musculotendinous junction)
common.rtpConsiderations: Restore full eccentric hamstring strength (especially at long muscle length); progressive reintroduction of high-speed running; Nordic curl protocol through RTP. Return-to-speed testing (flying sprint, NordBord) before maximal efforts.
common.source: Askling hamstring-strain literature; van Dyk et al.; Petersen 2011 Nordic hamstring RCT

common.name: Quadriceps (rectus femoris) strain — acute
common.incidence: moderate — second most common acute sprint injury
common.severity: moderate (grade I–II typical; grade III rare but serious)
common.mechanism: Explosive hip flexion and knee extension during swing/acceleration overloads the rectus femoris, especially near musculotendinous junction; block start position can stretch the rectus under maximal demand.
common.rtpConsiderations: Progressive loaded hip-flexion + knee-extension work; graded return to acceleration and block work before maximal speed.

common.name: Hip flexor strain (iliopsoas/rectus femoris — proximal)
common.incidence: moderate — associated with block start and high-stride-frequency demands
common.mechanism: Forceful hip flexion at the block start and swing phase overloads the iliopsoas and proximal rectus femoris under stretched-shortened cycle loading.

modifiable: weak hip flexors relative to demand

common.rtpConsiderations: Active hip-flexor strengthening through range; graded block-start reintroduction.

common.name: Patellar tendinopathy
common.incidence: lower (relative to field sports) — repetitive plyometric training + heavy quad loading in gym
common.mechanism: Cumulative patellar tendon load from plyometric work, depth jumps, and heavy squatting; aggravated by training volume spikes.
common.rtpConsiderations: Isometric + heavy slow resistance loading; patellar tendon load management; plyometric volume reduction.

injuryProfile.summary: ACUTE high-force injuries dominate — hamstring strain (biceps femoris) is the defining sprint injury, driven by eccentric loading deficit and speed-work demands. Hip-flexor and quad strains are secondary. Overuse is less common than in distance but plyometric volume can drive patellar tendinopathy. Hamstring eccentric strength (Nordic curls, NordBord testing) and load management are the primary modifiable levers.

positions.name: 100 m (pure speed / ATP-PC)
positions.role: The ultimate test of maximal neuromuscular speed — reaction, acceleration, and top-end velocity.
positions.movementDemands: Explosive block start; 0–30 m acceleration (horizontal force orientation); 30–60 m velocity build; 60–100 m maximal-velocity maintenance.
positions.runningDemands: Peak velocities 10–12 m/s (elite); contact times ~85–100 ms at top speed; arm drive and leg stiffness decisive.
positions.bodyComposition: Lean, extremely powerful; fast-twitch dominant; minimal non-propulsive mass.
gymPriorities: maximal explosive power (power clean, depth jump)
horizontal force production (sled push, back squat)
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Very high CNS demand per session — recovery must be managed. No heavy gym within 24 h of maximal speed work.

positions.name: 200 m (speed + speed-endurance)
positions.role: Combines peak speed of the 100 m with a decisive speed-endurance component in the second 100 m.
positions.movementDemands: Curved start on bend; maximal acceleration; velocity maintenance under rising glycolytic demand.
positions.runningDemands: Peak velocities similar to 100 m; greater lactate production in the back straight; arm drive and pelvic stability under fatigue.
positions.bodyComposition: Lean, powerful; similar to 100 m but some tolerance for glycolytic capacity.
gymPriorities: power and strength as per 100 m
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Higher metabolic demand than 100 m — recovery between sessions must account for glycolytic fatigue.

positions.name: 400 m (speed-endurance / lactate tolerance)
positions.role: The 'long sprint' — a contest of speed-endurance, lactate buffering, and velocity maintenance under extreme metabolic fatigue.
positions.movementDemands: Full 400 m at maximal sustainable effort; late-race mechanics degradation under lactate; stride length maintenance critical.
positions.runningDemands: Sustained near-maximal effort for 40–50 s (elite) or up to ~70 s; glycolytic peak; some aerobic contribution (~15–20%) in final 100 m.
positions.bodyComposition: Lean but tolerates slightly more aerobic capacity than 100 m specialists.
gymPriorities: hamstring eccentric strength (highest priority — fatigue magnifies risk)
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Extreme metabolic load — requires 48–72 h recovery after a maximal 400 m effort. Gym scheduling must account for glycolytic fatigue.

assessments.name: 30 m flying sprint (maximal velocity)
assessments.purpose: Measure peak sprint velocity — the primary performance output. Timing gates at 30 m with a 30 m run-in gives a clean flying-speed measurement.
assessments.source: Haugen 2019 sprint-performance testing; World Athletics testing standards

assessments.name: NordBord / eccentric hamstring strength (Nordic curl test)
assessments.purpose: Measure bilateral eccentric hamstring force output — the primary modifiable risk factor for hamstring strain. Essential for return-to-sport and ongoing monitoring.
equipment: NordBord or equivalent eccentric dynamometer; alternative: Nordic curl with force plate
assessments.source: Petersen 2011 Nordic hamstring RCT; van Dyk eccentric-strength testing

assessments.name: Countermovement jump (CMJ) / reactive strength index (RSI)
assessments.purpose: Lower-body power and neuromuscular freshness monitoring — CMJ correlates with sprint acceleration; RSI reflects leg stiffness relevant to maximal-velocity mechanics.

targets.elite: CMJ >50 cm (men), >40 cm (women) indicative; track trend

assessments.name: 10 m split + 30 m acceleration test
assessments.purpose: Separate block-start/early-acceleration (10 m) from general acceleration (30 m) — identifies whether limitations are in block mechanics or open-sprint mechanics.

assessments.name: Horizontal force-velocity profile (sled push / radar)
assessments.purpose: Profile whether the athlete is force-deficient or velocity-deficient in sprint mechanics — guides gym prescription (more strength vs more plyometric/ballistic work).

targets.elite: optimise F-v ratio; identify dominant deficit

equipment: sled + friction-coefficient calibration + timing gates; or radar gun
assessments.source: Morin & Samozino force-velocity profiling for sprinting

assessments.name: Hip flexor flexibility + single-leg hip-extension ROM
assessments.purpose: Identify hip-flexor tightness limiting stride length and increasing hamstring/hip-flexor injury risk; Thomas test + modified Thomas.
assessments.source: sprint-biomechanics and injury-risk literature; expert consensus

assessments.name: Reactive strength index (drop jump RSI)
assessments.purpose: Quantify leg stiffness and ground-contact efficiency — critical for maximal-velocity sprint mechanics; high RSI correlates with shorter contact times.
equipment: jump mat / force plate; box 30–40 cm

highest: sprint mechanics (A-skip, B-skip, wall drill, falling start)
youth.trainingEmphasis: Mechanics-first: sprint drills, acceleration, bodyweight strength. Build the coordination and connective-tissue base. Protect the hamstring via basic hip-hinge and Nordic introductions.
commonMistakes: too much high-intensity volume on developing connective tissue

highest: strength base (trap-bar DL, back squat, hip thrust)
lowest: too much 400 m before power base is built
development.trainingEmphasis: Build the force-velocity foundation. Introduce Olympic lifting when technically ready. Establish Nordic curl habit. Grow plyometric complexity with a strength base.
commonMistakes: skipping heavy strength work in favour of more speed sessions

lowest: high-soreness exercises within 48 h of key speed sessions
senior.trainingEmphasis: Individualise force-velocity profile; maintain strength/power at low fatigue in-season; protect the hamstring; optimise the competition taper.
commonMistakes: dropping Nordic curls when programme busy
poor taper (too much volume, not enough intensity)

elite.trainingEmphasis: Data-led force-velocity individualisation; minimal-effective in-season gym; protect the hamstring at all costs; nail the taper.
commonMistakes: testing without acting on force-velocity results

lowest: maximal CNS load at high volume
aggressive plyometric volume on ageing tendons
masters.trainingEmphasis: Maintain force-velocity qualities conservatively; increase recovery time; prioritise connective-tissue health and hamstring prehab.

offSeason.primaryObjective: Build maximal strength + general power foundation; address injury risk factors (hamstring eccentric strength deficit) and mobility limitations.
offSeason.trainingEmphasis: Maximal strength (back squat, trap-bar DL, hip thrust), hypertrophy if needed, Nordic curls, general plyometrics, sprint mechanics (technical, sub-maximal).

preSeason.primaryObjective: Convert strength base to explosive power and sprint-specific RFD; build speed-endurance for 200/400 m; sharpen block start.
preSeason.trainingEmphasis: Power/Olympic lifts, depth jumps, sled work, speed-endurance sessions; begin race-pace track work; reduce gym volume as track intensity rises.

competition.primaryObjective: Maintain explosive power; protect the hamstring; execute the taper into key competitions.
competition.trainingEmphasis: Reduced gym volume (2 sessions), maintained intensity; plyometric priming; full Nordic curl maintenance; no novel high-fatigue exercises.

playoffs.primaryObjective: Peak taper for target championship — heats + semis + finals over multiple days.
playoffs.trainingEmphasis: Minimal-volume high-intensity priming; recovery between rounds; CNS priming only on race days.
testingRecommendations: readiness monitoring only — no fatiguing tests

recovery.primaryObjective: Full physical and psychological recovery; address any carried injuries.
recovery.trainingEmphasis: Low-intensity activity, mobility, light cross-training; eccentric hamstring maintenance if injury-free; medical review of carried issues.

oneMatchPerWeek.pattern: Built around 1–2 quality track sessions (maximal speed and/or speed-endurance); gym placed to NOT fatigue the CNS or hamstring before track quality work.
oneMatchPerWeek.heavyDay: early-week (Monday/Tuesday), away from the key track speed session
oneMatchPerWeek.powerDay: mid-week (small power/plyometric session after speed work — priming carryover)
oneMatchPerWeek.recoveryDay: day after heavy track or heavy gym; pre-race day is light
oneMatchPerWeek.mobilityDay: daily (hip flexors, hamstring, hip external rotation)
oneMatchPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: Nordic curls + hip-flexor + single-leg stability embedded 2–3×/week, not adjacent to maximal speed
oneMatchPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Heavy gym early-week → quality speed session mid-week → light/technical → race → recovery.
preferExplosiveWorkDays: dedicated gym day mid-week away from racing

twoMatchesPerWeek.pattern: Multi-round meet (heats + semis + finals): recovery-first between rounds; no heavy gym.
twoMatchesPerWeek.powerDay: brief CNS priming on race morning if used
twoMatchesPerWeek.recoveryDay: between heats/semis/finals and after each day
twoMatchesPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Warm-up → heat → recovery → semi → recovery → final. Gym is priming or none.

tournamentOrCongested.pattern: Multi-day championships with multiple rounds: pure freshness management — gym is activation/priming only.
tournamentOrCongested.typicalLoadingPattern: Protect recovery and mechanics quality between rounds; no development loading.
preferExplosiveWorkDays: race-morning primers only (jumps, skips, drills — no fatigue)

transfersWell: heavy back squat / trap-bar deadlift (maximal force production base)
Nordic curl / RDL (hamstring eccentric strength — injury prevention + posterior chain power)
power clean / hang clean (triple extension RFD — direct sprint mechanics transfer)
depth jump / drop jump (reactive strength / leg stiffness)
broad jump + bounding A-skip (horizontal power / sprint-specific)
sled push (overloaded acceleration mechanics — horizontal force emphasis)
double-leg / single-leg pogo (Achilles/tendon stiffness — maximal-velocity mechanics)
Pallof press + dead bug (core anti-rotation/anti-extension under sprint mechanics)
limitedValue: non-specific hypertrophy (adds non-propulsive mass without power gain)
machine-based isolation work replacing compound power movements
heavy eccentric work within 48 h of maximal speed sessions (pre-fatigues hamstring/CNS)
long steady-state cardio (no transfer; adds mass and fatigue without sprint benefit)
high-volume plyometrics on top of a full track week (cumulative tendon / CNS overload)
essentialMovementPatterns: single-leg hip hinge (SL hinge — unilateral hamstring)
accessoryPriorities: Nordic curl / eccentric hamstring (priority #1 — injury prevention)
hip abductor stability (lateral band walk, Copenhagen)
gymPhilosophy.singleLegEmphasis: Moderate-high — sprint is a unilateral cyclic task; single-leg hinge, step-up, and single-leg calf build the unilateral hip/posterior-chain robustness that reduces asymmetry-driven injury risk.
gymPhilosophy.olympicLiftingSuitability: Valuable — power/hang clean delivers triple-extension RFD that directly maps to sprint block start and early-acceleration mechanics. Recommend where technical competency exists.
gymPhilosophy.plyometricEmphasis: High — maximal-intent depth jumps, broad jumps, bounds, and sprint-specific bounding are core to sprint development. Progress off a strength base; schedule away from maximal speed sessions.
gymPhilosophy.coreTrainingPhilosophy: Anti-extension and anti-rotation dominate — the pelvis and trunk must transmit force from the ground through each stride without energy leakage. Pallof press, dead bug, hollow hold. Minimal loaded spinal-flexion volume.
gymPhilosophy.rotationalTraining: Low-moderate — arm-drive mechanics and trunk counter-rotation are trained via sprint drills and med-ball work rather than heavy rotation exercises.
gymPhilosophy.isometricTraining: Useful in season and rehab — isometric hip-hinge holds, Spanish squat (patellar tendon), wall-assisted Nordic holds; low-fatigue in-season maintenance.
gymPhilosophy.tempoRecommendations: Explosive concentric intent on all power/plyometric work; controlled eccentric on hamstring-loading exercises (Nordic, RDL); avoid grinding fatigue near quality track sessions.
gymPhilosophy.velocityRecommendations: Max intent on power movements at relatively low volume in-season. Speed-strength continuum: heavy/slow in off-season → power/fast in pre-season → plyometric/reactive in competition phase.

exercises.name: Nordic hamstring curl
exercises.primaryAdaptation: eccentric hamstring strength (biceps femoris) — the primary sprint injury-prevention exercise
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: posterior chain strength and hamstring hypertrophy

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift (RDL)
exercises.movementPattern: hip hinge — eccentric hamstring under load
exercises.primaryAdaptation: hamstring + glute strength at long muscle length
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: posterior chain hypertrophy; sprint posterior-chain robustness

exercises.name: Power clean
exercises.primaryAdaptation: explosive power / RFD — direct block-start and acceleration transfer
exercises.jointLoading: moderate (wrist/elbow on catch; low if hang)

exercises.name: Back squat
exercises.movementPattern: bilateral squat — maximal force production base
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: core stability; relative strength base for sprint force

exercises.name: Hip thrust (barbell / banded)
exercises.primaryAdaptation: glute maximus strength + power — horizontal force production specificity

exercises.name: Depth jump (reactive / reactive plyometric)
exercises.primaryAdaptation: reactive strength / leg stiffness — maximal-velocity contact mechanics

exercises.name: Broad jump (horizontal plyometric)
exercises.primaryAdaptation: horizontal lower-body power (block start + early-acceleration transfer)

exercises.name: Sled push (resisted sprint)
exercises.movementPattern: resisted horizontal triple extension — force-orientation training
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: posterior chain and quad loading under sprint posture

exercises.name: Double-leg pogo jump
exercises.primaryAdaptation: Achilles tendon stiffness + ankle plantar-flexion power — maximal-velocity ground-contact mechanics

exercises.name: Pallof press (anti-rotation core)
exercises.primaryAdaptation: trunk anti-rotation — force-transfer efficiency during each sprint stride

exercises.name: Bounding / A-skip
exercises.movementPattern: sprint-specific cyclic power (horizontal bounding, high knee cycling)
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: hip-flexor + glute activation in sprint-specific pattern

exercises.name: Lateral band walk
exercises.primaryAdaptation: glute medius + hip abductor stability — single-leg stance phase robustness

exercises.name: Dead bug (anti-extension core)
exercises.primaryAdaptation: core anti-extension — maintains sprint posture and force-transfer efficiency
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: low-back protection under repeated ground-contact loading

warningSigns: proximal posterior thigh tightness / soreness after speed work
reduced Nordic curl force output vs baseline
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Nordic curl 2×/week year-round; RDL 2×/week; single-leg hinge 1–2×/week
exercisesToAvoid: heavy RDL or Nordic within 48 h of maximal speed session
novel high-load eccentric without progressive build
monitoringRecommendations: monthly NordBord bilateral force + L/R ratio
weekly hamstring soreness check before high-speed sessions
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Petersen 2011 Nordic hamstring RCT; Askling; van Dyk

riskFactors: weak hip flexors relative to demand
warningSigns: anterior hip or proximal quad tightness / soreness
discomfort on explosive hip-flexion drills (A-skip, block start)
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Hip-flexor mobility daily (dynamic warm-up); unilateral hip work 2×/week
exercisesToAvoid: aggressive loaded hip-flexion exercises on a fatigued athlete before speed sessions
monitoringRecommendations: soreness check on anterior hip before block work

warningSigns: anterior knee pain below the kneecap especially after plyometric sessions
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Progressive tendon loading 2×/week; avoid plyometric volume spikes
exercisesToAvoid: depth jumps on hard surfaces without adequate tendon preparation
monitoringRecommendations: anterior knee soreness NRS before and after sessions
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: patellar tendinopathy load-management literature; expert consensus

decisionRules.if: readiness score low (poor sleep + high soreness + low wellness) on any training day
decisionRules.then: autoregulate down one step: replace high-speed / heavy gym session with a technical/drill session or active recovery; do not attempt maximal speed or maximal strength when poorly recovered

decisionRules.if: athlete reports systemic illness (fever, below-neck symptoms, infectious illness)
decisionRules.then: withhold all training until symptom-free; resume gradually — no high-speed or heavy strength work for 48 h after symptom resolution

decisionRules.if: weekly sprint-session volume (speed work m / session RPE) ACWR > 1.5 vs 28-day chronic baseline
decisionRules.then: cap high-speed running volume this week; do not add gym volume; prioritise recovery; flag for coach review
decisionRules.source: Gabbett 2016 (methodology contested — Impellizzeri 2020, Lolli 2019); applied as a soft monitoring input

decisionRules.if: in taper phase (1–2 weeks before target competition)
decisionRules.then: reduce total volume substantially (~40–60%) while MAINTAINING intensity; keep low-volume plyometric and strength priming; maximise recovery; no novel or high-soreness exercises

decisionRules.if: race day or within 24 hours of competition
decisionRules.then: gym/track work is CNS priming only (a few jumps, short accelerations, sprint drills) or none; no strength development; complete warm-up only

decisionRules.if: athlete reports posterior thigh soreness (NRS ≥3/10) or proximal hamstring tightness, OR NordBord force drops >10% vs baseline
decisionRules.then: remove maximal-velocity sprint work and all heavy posterior-chain loading; switch to sub-maximal technical running (≤80% effort), light hip-hinge mobility, and non-fatiguing prehab (isometric hamstring, gentle RDL); flag for physio review if persisting >3 days

decisionRules.if: a maximal-velocity or speed-endurance track session is scheduled within 24 hours
decisionRules.then: avoid heavy lower-body gym (squats, RDL, Nordic curl, depth jumps, sled) the day before — preserve CNS and posterior-chain freshness for speed quality; a light upper-body or core session is permissible
decisionRules.source: expert consensus (speed-session priority sequencing); CNS-fatigue literature

decisionRules.if: CMJ height >10% below rolling 4-week baseline on two consecutive measures
decisionRules.then: treat as accumulated neuromuscular fatigue: reduce CNS-demanding training (maximal speed, Olympic lifts, plyometrics); emphasise recovery; re-test in 48–72 h before returning to high-CNS work
hold strength/power gym work at minimal effective volume (2 low-volume high-quality sessions per week); maintain Nordic curl; maintain plyometric priming; avoid high-DOMS exercises near racing

acwr.model: Acute (7-day) : chronic (28-day) of sprint-volume load (high-speed metres × RPE); rolling EWMA preferred to reduce day-to-day variability
acwr.source: Gabbett 2016 — methodology contested (Impellizzeri 2020, Lolli 2019); used as a soft monitoring input only

loadManagement.weeklyProgressionGuideline: Avoid >~10–15% week-to-week spike in sprint volume (high-speed metres) or plyometric/gym volume; the hamstring under maximal load is the primary risk tissue.

gymVolumeRanges.offSeason: high (3 sessions; strength + power + prehab foundation)
gymVolumeRanges.inSeason: low-moderate maintenance (2 sessions; low volume, high quality, no DOMS near racing)

loadManagement.minimumEffectiveVolume: ~2 low-volume gym sessions/week sustain power/strength in-season; Nordic curl must NOT drop below 2×/week year-round.
loadManagement.maximumAdaptiveVolume: Off-season — build maximal strength and power foundation here, when distance from competition allows full recovery.
loadManagement.maximumRecoverableVolume: Constrained by hamstring recovery and total sprint-session volume; gym must never compromise the quality of maximal-speed track work or hamstring health.
loadManagement.deloadRecommendations: Planned deload every 3–4 weeks in development phases; auto-deload on hamstring soreness flag, CMJ drop, or ACWR >1.5. Competition taper is a planned performance deload.
loadManagement.progressionRules: Progress gym load when quality met at target RPE and hamstring is symptom-free; prefer intensity over volume in-season; progress plyometric complexity only after strength competency.
loadManagement.regressionRules: On hamstring soreness or red readiness, drop speed-session volume first and reduce posterior-chain gym load; never schedule heavy lower-body gym within 24 h of maximal speed.
loadManagement.missedSessionRules: Do not stack missed speed sessions; resume at planned level. After time off (esp. hamstring injury), rebuild speed volume gradually over 2–4 weeks with NordBord checks.
loadManagement.source: Mujika/Bosquet (taper); Gabbett (load — contested); Rønnestad (maintenance); Askling/Petersen (hamstring); expert consensus

thresholds.when: NRS ≥3/10 posterior thigh or proximal hamstring tightness
thresholds.modifier: remove maximal speed + heavy posterior-chain gym; prehab only; flag for physio

thresholds.when: high prior CNS/sprint load + short recovery (<36 h)
thresholds.modifier: lower today's speed or gym load
reduce CNS-demanding training (max speed, Olympic lifts, depth jumps)
treat as accumulating fatigue; ease sprint and gym load
possible fatigue or illness — caution before high-intensity work
reduce intensity; prioritise sleep and recovery

readinessModel.notes: Hamstring soreness is elevated to a top-priority, sprint-specific readiness input — it should GATE all high-speed and heavy posterior-chain work. CMJ is an unusually important objective signal here (CNS/power sensitivity). Subjective wellness + sleep + prior load carry the most general weight. Raw vitals (HRV/RHR/sleep) stay private to the athlete; the coach sees only the derived readiness score.

coachDashboard.principle: Coach sees DERIVED signals and availability only — never an individual athlete's raw HRV, sleep, or resting HR. Aggregated, plain-English, action-oriented.
weeklyReports: speed volume vs plan (per athlete/event group)
coachDashboard.trafficLightIndicators: Per-athlete green/amber/red from the derived readiness + load state (no raw numbers shown).
coachDashboard.privacyNote: All per-athlete entries here are DERIVED (readiness score, load_state, ACWR, adherence %, injury availability). Raw vitals are excluded by design and enforced by the schema validator.

taper improves sprint performance — reduce volume, maintain intensity (Mujika/Padilla; Bosquet 2007)
subjective wellness is a sensitive readiness indicator (Saw 2016)
in-season strength can be maintained at low volume (Rønnestad & Mujika 2014)
horizontal force profiling distinguishes force-deficient from velocity-deficient sprinters (Morin & Samozino)
weakEvidence: exact ACWR thresholds for sprint injury risk (contested methodology)
specific gym volume thresholds for peak sprint performance
optimal Nordic curl dose (frequency/volume) for prevention vs performance
precise energy-system percentages for each sprint event
areasRequiringExpertJudgement: force-velocity profile prescription (individual force vs velocity deficit)
taper duration and magnitude (event-specific, individual-variation is large)
managing heavy gym work alongside a full speed-work week
RTP decision-making after hamstring strain (graded testing vs time-based)
areasRequiringFutureResearch: optimal Nordic curl programme within a full sprint-training week
long-term hamstring health in masters sprinters
AI-based real-time sprint-mechanics feedback from wearables
personalised force-velocity profiling in sub-elite populations
potentialRisksIfMisimplemented: scheduling heavy posterior-chain gym within 24 h of maximal speed work (hamstring injury risk)
dropping Nordic curls in-season when the programme gets busy (removes the primary prevention lever)
treating ACWR as a hard rule rather than a soft signal
exposing raw vitals to coaches (privacy + trust breach)
botched taper — too much volume retained, performance suppressed

kpis.name: Readiness
kpis.measurementMethod: Composite of subjective wellness + sleep + prior load + hamstring soreness (+ optional CMJ and HRV trend), normalised to baseline
kpis.source: Saw 2016; derived score (raw vitals stay private)

kpis.name: Weekly consistency
kpis.measurementMethod: % prescribed sessions (track + gym + prehab + check-ins) completed

kpis.name: Training availability
kpis.measurementMethod: fit / modified / out (status only — esp. hamstring)

kpis.name: Race time (event performance)
kpis.measurementMethod: Race / time-trial time for athlete's event (100/200/400 m)

kpis.name: CMJ power (neuromuscular freshness + power trend)
kpis.measurementMethod: Countermovement jump height or flight-time (jump mat / force plate)
kpis.targetRange: within 10% of 4-week baseline for fatigue monitoring; trend upward for power development
kpis.source: Claudino 2017 (CMJ neuromuscular monitoring); Seitz 2014 (strength → sprint power)

kpis.name: Eccentric hamstring strength (NordBord)
kpis.measurementMethod: NordBord bilateral eccentric hamstring force (N/kg) + L/R symmetry index; or Nordic curl max-breakpoint force
kpis.source: Petersen 2011; van Dyk eccentric-strength testing literature

kpis.name: Sleep
kpis.measurementMethod: Wearable / self-report sleep duration and quality

kpis.name: Resting HR
kpis.measurementMethod: Morning resting heart rate vs personal baseline
kpis.source: expert consensus (PRIVATE — athlete-only; rolls into readiness)

performanceScore.philosophy: Reflects progress toward the explosive speed and power demands of competitive sprinting, weighted to reward the qualities that actually determine race outcomes (power, speed, availability) while penalising injury risk, hamstring fragility, and excessive fatigue — never rewarding training through injury.

components.rationale: Consistent training attendance is the foundation of sprint adaptation.
Hamstring-healthy availability is the strongest performance lever — injured sprinters don't improve.
Race-time improvement is the primary performance outcome.
CMJ power tracks the explosive neuromuscular quality that drives sprint speed.
Eccentric hamstring strength is a leading indicator of hamstring resilience — trainable and protective.
Penalises chronic fatigue and poor recovery; keeps the score sustainable.
Mild penalty for load-spiking patterns that increase injury risk.

guardrails: never increases for training through hamstring pain, red readiness, or injury
consistency + availability dominate so the score can't be gamed by occasional maximal efforts
CMJ drop or poor recovery caps the score when neuromuscular fatigue is high
performanceScore.explainability: Each component is shown with its contribution so the sprinter sees exactly why the score moved and what to work on next.

gamification.name: Hamstring-healthy weeks
gamification.rewards: Consecutive weeks training and racing without hamstring soreness — tied to the sport's primary injury risk.

gamification.name: Nordic curl streak
gamification.rewards: Unbroken weeks completing the Nordic curl programme — makes the most important prehab habit visible and rewarded.

gamification.name: Consistency streak
gamification.rewards: Unbroken weeks hitting prescribed track + gym sessions; rewards process over outcome.

gamification.name: Power milestone
gamification.rewards: CMJ personal bests — a direct, gym-driven proxy for sprint power that the athlete controls.

gamification.name: NordBord milestone
gamification.rewards: Eccentric hamstring force personal bests — protects the career while being a concrete achievement.

gamification.name: Personal-best milestones
gamification.rewards: Race-time PBs vs the athlete's own baseline — self-referenced, never leaderboard.

gamification.name: Testing-battery completion
gamification.rewards: Completing each testing block (CMJ / NordBord / split times) — encourages objective tracking.
